question: What does f do to plain lowercase words, mixed-case words, words with spaces, and simple alphanumeric strings — is it identity, case change, reversal, or some combination?
expect: If outputs equal inputs, f is identity on these. If case is flipped/upper/lowercased, we learn the case rule. If order reverses (e.g. 'olleh'), we learn reversal. If spaces are removed or words transformed separately, we learn tokenization behavior. Comparing 'hello' vs 'HELLO' vs 'hELLo' isolates case handling, and 'abc123' vs '123' isolates digit handling.

question: Does the +1 letter shift apply to the last character of the whole string, of each word, and what happens with punctuation, digits, and uppercase boundaries (z/Z wrap)?
expect: If shift is per whitespace-word last char: cat->cau, dog.->unchanged ('.' not letter), hi!->unchanged, yes?->unchanged, a1->unchanged, 1a->1b, Z->A (wrap) or unchanged, z->a (wrap) or unchanged, Buzz->BuzA? (last char z->a) or BuzA, test end.->tesu end. (last of 'end.' is '.', unchanged) vs 'tesu endt' if punctuation ignored. Comparing these pins down whether punctuation/digits block the shift, and whether z/Z wrap to a/A.

question: Does the last-character +1 shift skip over non-letter characters (e.g. trailing spaces, punctuation, or digits at the very end) or only apply when the final character is a letter, and does it look past trailing non-letters to shift the last letter?
expect: If only the literal last character matters (current model), all outputs equal inputs unchanged, since the last char is space/punctuation/digit. If the box instead shifts the last letter in the string ignoring trailing non-letters, outputs would be like 'hellp ', 'worle.', 'abd!', 'tesu ', 'cau1', 'dog9'->'doga'? etc. Comparing these reveals whether trailing spaces/punctuation/digits are skipped to find a letter to shift, which is a common ordinary-input case (words followed by spaces or punctuation).

question: Does the final-letter +1 shift apply to words ending in accented/non-ASCII letters or only to plain A-Z/a-z, and how are multi-character strings ending in a lone uppercase/lowercase boundary handled when the letter is at the very end after spaces?
expect: If only ASCII letters shift, accented endings stay unchanged (café, naïve, résumé, test é, über, Å, ä, ö). If Unicode letters shift like letters, they'd advance to the next code point (é→ê, ï→ð, etc.), revealing a broader rule. 'hello W' should become 'hello X' and 'hello w' should become 'hello x' under the current ASCII model; if instead the space blocks the shift, they'd stay unchanged, distinguishing 'last char only' from 'last letter after trailing spaces'.

question: Does the +1 shift apply only to the final character, or to the last letter of each word / every character, when the string contains multiple words or internal punctuation?
expect: If only the very last character is shifted (current model), outputs are 'ab ce', 'ab-ce', 'ab.ce', 'ab cd ef'->'ab cd ef'? no: 'ab cd eF'? Let's state: 'ab cd'->'ab ce', 'ab-cd'->'ab-ce', 'ab.cd'->'ab.ce', 'ab cd ef'->'ab cd eg', 'one two three'->'one two thref', 'a-b-c'->'a-b-d', 'hello, world'->'hello, worle', 'hello world!'->'hello world!', 'x y'->'x z', 'foo bar baz'->'foo bar baa'. Any output where an internal word's last letter is shifted (e.g. 'ab cd'->'ac cd' or 'ab ce' vs 'ac cd') would reveal per-word shifting; unchanged punctuation-ending strings confirm no look-past-trailing-nonletters.

question: Does the final-letter +1 shift apply only to the very last character of the whole string, or to the last letter of each whitespace-separated word, when a trailing word ends in a non-letter (punctuation/digit/space)?
expect: If only the whole-string last char matters, all outputs stay unchanged (trailing punctuation/digit). If the last letter of each word shifts, outputs become 'ab ce.', 'ab ce1', 'foo bar!', 'foo bar2', 'one two thref.', 'one two thref9', 'x z?', 'x z7', 'hello worle,', 'hello worle0'. This distinguishes whole-string vs per-word final-letter behavior and tells whether the shift looks past trailing non-letters within a word.

question: Does the +1 shift apply to the last letter of each whitespace-separated word independently, or only to the final character of the whole string, when there are multiple words and the final character is a letter?
expect: If each word's last letter shifts, outputs will be 'ab ce', 'one twp', 'foo bar baa', 'hello worle', 'a b d', 'cat dog'->'cat doh', 'x y a', 'red green bluf', 'ab cd ef gi', 'sun moon stas'. If only the whole-string final character shifts, outputs will be 'ab ce', 'one two', 'foo bar baz', 'hello world', 'a b c', 'cat dog', 'x y z', 'red green blue', 'ab cd ef gh', 'sun moon star'. E5 already showed multi-word shifting of each word's last letter, so this confirms and generalizes that on ordinary phrases.

question: Does the +1 shift apply to the last letter of each whitespace-separated word even when that word ends in punctuation or digits, i.e. does it look past trailing non-letters inside a word to shift the word's last letter?
expect: The model already predicts these unchanged (trailing non-letter means no shift). If they come back unchanged, it confirms the shift is purely on the final character of each word (no looking past trailing non-letters). If instead the last letter before the punctuation/digit shifts (e.g. 'ab cd.' -> 'ab ce.'), that would reveal a look-past-trailing-non-letter behavior the current model misses.

question: Does the shift apply to the last character of each whitespace-separated word when a word ends in a letter but the whole string ends in a non-letter (e.g. trailing space or punctuation after a later word), and does an internal word ending in a non-letter get skipped?
expect: If the rule is 'shift the last letter of each word, skipping trailing non-letters within it', then 'ab cd ' -> 'ab ce ' (word 'cd' still shifted, trailing space untouched), 'ab cd!' -> 'ab ce!', 'foo bar baz.' -> 'foo bar baa.', etc. If instead only the final character of the whole string is considered, these all stay unchanged because the string ends in non-letter. Comparing the two outcomes distinguishes whole-string-last-char vs per-word-last-letter rules on ordinary multi-word inputs with trailing punctuation/space.

question: Does the +1 shift apply to the last letter of each whitespace-separated word even when that word ends in a non-letter, i.e. does it look past trailing punctuation/digits inside a word to shift the word's last letter?
expect: If the box only shifts the very last character when it is a letter (current model), outputs will be identical to inputs: ["ab cd.","ab cd1","foo bar!","foo bar2","one two three.","one two three9","x y?","x y7","hello world,","hello world0"]. If instead it shifts the last letter of each whitespace-separated word looking past trailing non-letters, outputs would be ["ab ce.","ab ce1","foo bar!","foo bas2","one two thref.","one two thref9","x z?","x z7","hello worle,","hello worle0"]. This distinguishes per-word letter shifting from whole-string last-character shifting on ordinary multi-word inputs.

question: When a string has multiple words, does the +1 shift apply to the last letter of every whitespace-separated word, or only to the final character of the whole string — testing with words containing internal punctuation/digits and mixed trailing characters to see if earlier words are ever shifted.
expect: If only the very last character shifts, outputs would be 'ab-cd eG', 'ab.cd eG', 'ab1cd eG', 'foo-bar baA', 'foo.bar baA', 'one-two threE', 'a1b c2E', 'hello-world foO', 'x9y z8X', 'cat-dog birD' (last letter +1). If the last letter of each word shifts, earlier words ending in letters would also change, e.g. 'ab-cd ef'->'ab-ce eg'? Actually punctuation blocks: 'ab-cd' ends in 'd' so would become 'ab-ce'; 'ab.cd'->'ab.ce'; 'foo-bar'->'foo-bas'. This distinguishes whether internal words are processed when they end in a letter before punctuation/digits, clarifying the per-word vs whole-string rule.

question: Does the +1 shift apply to the last letter of each whitespace-separated word independently, or only to the final character of the whole string, when there are multiple words and the final character is a letter?
expect: If only the final character shifts, outputs would be 'ab ce', 'one twp', 'foo bar baa', etc. (matching E7). If every word's last letter shifts, we'd see 'ac ce', 'onf twp', etc. E7 already showed only the final character shifts, so this would confirm that; a different result would overturn it.
